Southern mountain cavy (Microcavia australis) is a small, diurnal rodent inhabiting arid and semi-arid regions of southern South America, where it forms complex social groups and constructs extensive burrow systems. Neonates emerge at a remarkably small body size, with recorded birth masses averaging approximately 30 grams [Wwb = approximately 30 grams] in wild populations. This modest initial mass is typical of many hystricognath rodents, though it imposes a significant energetic demand on lactating females during the early postpartum period. Under the controlled thermal conditions of a laboratory setting maintained at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], a consistent pattern of developmental milestones has been documented. For instance, the gestation period, the interval between copulation and parturition, proceeds for 54 days [tg = 54 days] at this temperature, a duration that aligns closely with predictions from allometric equations for rodents of comparable adult body mass at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. The sustained warmth appears to be critical for normal embryogenesis, as cooler environments can delay foetal development and reduce neonatal viability in captive colonies.

Following parturition, the suckling juvenile phase is relatively abbreviated in this species. The transition to nutritional independence, marked by the cessation of lactation and initiation of solid food consumption, occurs at weaning. In field studies and captive observations conducted at a stable ambient temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], weaning is completed approximately 21 days after birth [tx = approximately 21 days after birth]. This timing reflects the rapid growth trajectory characteristic of this cavy, allowing young to exploit the seasonally abundant herbaceous vegetation typical of their semiarid habitat. The pre-weaning period is a critical window of vulnerability; pups rely entirely on maternal milk, and their body mass increases substantially from the approximately 30 gram [Wwb = approximately 30 gram] neonatal weight. The relatively short lactation interval likely evolved as an adaptation to unpredictable resource availability, enabling females to allocate energy to subsequent reproductive events rather than protracted parental investment. The social structure of communal burrowing may also buffer weanlings against predation during this vulnerable phase.

Sexual maturation in female Microcavia australis occurs well after weaning, representing a distinct developmental transition linked to body condition and environmental cues. Under stable thermal regimes of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], captive-born females typically attain puberty at 45 days after birth [tp = 45 days after birth]. There is notable intraspecific variation around this central estimate; field-collected individuals from lower-quality habitats or harsher seasons may exhibit a delay, with documented values ranging from 40 to 50 days after birth (40-50 days after birth) [tp = 40-50 days after birth] at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This variability underscores the plasticity inherent in the species' life-history strategy, permitting females to defer reproductive investment until conditions are favorable for the successful rearing of a litter. The polygynous mating system common among cavies further suggests that early maturation may confer advantages in competitive social environments. The onset of gonadal activity coincides with nearly complete somatic growth, as females approach a substantial proportion of their ultimate adult body mass during this period of rapid morphological development.

Adult female body size in this species is modest but distinctly larger than that of the neonates, reflecting the considerable energetic investment required to reach reproductive maturity. The ultimate wet weight for females is approximately 326 grams [Wwi = approximately 326 grams], a value that places Microcavia australis among the medium-sized members of the Caviidae family. This asymptotic mass is typically achieved within the first year of life under adequate nutritional conditions and is sustained throughout the reproductive lifespan. The pronounced size disparity between the approximately 30 gram [Wwb = approximately 30 gram] neonate and the approximately 326 gram [Wwi = approximately 326 gram] adult female highlights the magnitude of post-natal growth required to complete the life cycle. This growth trajectory is likely constrained by the seasonal availability of high-quality forage in the Monte Desert and Patagonian steppe habitats, where plant productivity is episodic and driven by unpredictable rainfall patterns. Females that attain a larger body mass are often observed to produce more robust litters, linking adult size directly to maternal investment capacity.

Reproductive output in this cavy is characterized by relatively small litters and a slow pace of life typical of hystricognath rodents. Within a controlled environment maintained at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], females produce between 1 and 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 1 and 5 pups per litter]. This limited per-event fecundity is offset by the capacity for repeated breeding attempts across the extended breeding season; field studies indicate that females may produce up to 2.5 litters annually [F_R_i = up to 2.5 litters annually], though this frequency is highly dependent on resource availability. The maximum recorded longevity for the species under optimal captive conditions at this temperature is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, compared to smaller myomorph rodents, enables a multi-year reproductive window that can buffer against years of poor environmental conditions. The combination of small litters, extended lifespan, and relatively late maturation aligns well with a slow life-history continuum that has been proposed for other South American hystricognaths.
